title: Samson
lead: The last and most famous of the judges: a Nazirite from before birth, given superhuman strength by the Spirit of the LORD, drawn to Philistine women, betrayed by Delilah, blinded, and finally killed when he pulled down the temple of Dagon on the Philistines.

sections.b: Samson's story fills Judges 13–16. His birth is announced to a barren mother like Isaac's and John the Baptist's (Judges 13; Luke 1:7–15); compare Samuel's. His strength comes when the Spirit of the LORD "sweeps down" on him (Judges 14:6, 19; 15:14), and it leaves when his Nazirite hair is cut and the LORD leaves him (Judges 16:20). He fights the Philistines alone and dies in a last act of revenge (Judges 16:28–30). Hebrews 11:32 names him among the heroes of faith. Jewish tradition honors him as a judge while drawing a lesson from his fall: "Samson went after his eyes, so the Philistines put out his eyes" (Mishnah Sotah 1:8). In Western art and music, from Milton's Samson Agonistes to Saint-Saëns's opera, Samson and Delilah became the pattern of the strong man undone by love.
